L1_fencing_owner_equality_only.fact: checkpoint_stage and _finish_claim authorise by claim_owner = worker_id AND teardown_id only. Neither checks claim_expires_at > now, so a worker whose lease has expired but not yet been taken over can still write. claim_due keeps teardown_id through COALESCE(teardown_id, $4) (line 296), so teardown_id is not a fence either
L1_fencing_owner_equality_only.note: reusing teardown_id is deliberate and must stay: it is the provider idempotency key, so a takeover re-drives the same teardown. Do not rotate it. The fence must be a separate monotonic claim_fencing_token
L1_fencing_owner_equality_only.restart_interaction: worker_id defaults to f'reaper-{uuid4()}' per process (environment_lifecycle.py:168), so today a restarted process cannot match its old incarnation's claim. Owner-equality becomes unsafe the moment anyone configures a stable worker_id (hostname or pod name). The fencing token closes that for any worker_id scheme

L2_zombie_stage_after_takeover.fact: a stage runs in asyncio.to_thread and cannot be cancelled. If the lease expires mid-stage, a second worker claims and re-runs the same destructive stage concurrently. The zombie's later checkpoint raises ValueError outside the try block (line 346), which aborts the pass with only a log line. Adapters therefore must be idempotent (P1 guarantees partly), and P2-1's killable executor plus fencing are the fix
L2_zombie_stage_after_takeover.thread_pool_exhaustion: each hung to_thread holds a default-executor worker (min(32, cpu+4)), starving every other to_thread caller in the process

L3_optimistic_conflict_surfaces_as_500.fact: replace() raises bare ValueError on a version mismatch. record_heartbeat/record_activity do not catch it, so a concurrent reaper claim (which bumps version) turns a heartbeat into HTTP 500
L3_optimistic_conflict_surfaces_as_500.falsifiable_requirement: P2-1: retry once on conflict (preserved test); if the retry also conflicts, return 409 Conflict, never 500

L4_reaping_pass_aborts_on_one_conflict.fact: `except ValueError: raise` means that when two replicas evaluate the same expiring row, the loser aborts evaluate_reaping before claim_due runs, so no teardown is claimed that tick on that replica

L7_restart_recovery_latency.fact: recovery happens through lease expiry plus the next reaper tick (the first tick waits interval_seconds after start, per commit 0a9bde8a). The durable prefix in teardown_stages_completed resumes from the earliest uncompleted stage (lines 312-314). Worst-case recovery latency = claim_ttl_seconds (>= stage_timeout_seconds * (len(ORDERED_STAGES)+1)) + interval_seconds
L7_restart_recovery_latency.sp_p2_divergence: SP-P2 says 'query PostgreSQL for incomplete checkpoints upon startup'. With more than one replica, a starting process cannot know a peer is dead, so startup must not steal unexpired claims. Lease expiry is the only safe signal. Recommend the Governor read SP-P2 as 'startup schedules a pass that resumes expired claims', with a test bounding the latency

L8_clock_source.fact: lease comparisons use the caller's Python `now` ($1), not the database now(). With several replicas, clock skew between them skews lease expiry. The optimistic lock uses an integer version (no timestamp round-trip, so no microsecond/nanosecond divergence)
L8_clock_source.recommendation: P2-1 may keep app-clock injection for tests, but the Postgres store should compare against the DB clock (or document the skew bound)
